report:
Revenue rose 18.7% on 1.3% fewer orders, but every year-on-year change graded WATCH
## Executive summary
- The data is 300 orders placed between January 2024 and December 2025, each with an order date, a region, a revenue amount and a unit count — 1,034 average revenue in the strongest region against 840 in the weakest.
- Revenue rose 18.7% (128,256 in the year before to 152,214 in the latest year) while order rows fell 1.3% (151 to 149) and units rose 1.6% (3,126 to 3,176); all five year-on-year comparisons are graded WATCH, with intervals that straddle zero.
- Average order revenue of 1,034 in North against 840 in West is the only difference the engine puts a range on, a gap of 194 (95% range 17.3 to 387).
- Units, not region, carries order revenue: Spearman 0.976 between units and revenue over 300 rows, and a model that loses R squared 0.949 when units is removed against 0.0139 when region is.
- Outside retail demand was firm, with US retail sales up from the same period a year ago [S4], but the engine's intervals are too wide to tie this year's 18.7% to it.
- No forecast is offered: 24 months of history is short of the 36 the engine requires, and it makes no monthly forecast of revenue, rows or units.
## The headline: Every year-on-year change is a watch, not a result
The five headline comparisons all point the same way but none clears the engine's bar, because the intervals are wider than the moves. Average revenue for the average month moved 853.6 to 1,016.3, +19.1% (interval -24.9% to +113.9%), and average units 20.8 to 21.2, +1.8% (interval -31.4% to +47.3%). Every interval contains zero, so the engine grades each change WATCH and flags that in simulated series with strong momentum it can underestimate the change.
## What drove it: The money moved per order, not through more orders
The average month's revenue rose 19.1% while the average month's units rose 1.8% and the order count fell 1.3% — value per order, not traffic. That is the shape of a value story: 853.6 to 1,016.3 in average monthly revenue against 20.8 to 21.2 in average monthly units, with two fewer order rows in the latest year. The engine's own reading is that with only region, date and units as context, nothing here separates product mix, customer type or discounting from a genuine shift in what customers bought, and it grades the move WATCH rather than settling it.
## Other findings: Order value is highest in North and lowest in West
North's average order is 1,034 (95% range 917 to 1,158, 75 rows) and West's is 840 (77 rows), a gap of 194 (95% range 17.3 to 387) — the one regional difference the engine carries with a range that excludes zero. East sits at 1,028 (71 rows, 896 to 1,151) and South at 847 (77 rows, 738 to 950). Medians tell a sharper version of the same split: North 1,186 against West 781, so the heavy orders pull North's mean further from its middle than West's.
[CHART:1]
[TABLE:1]
## Other findings: 2025's regional totals concentrate in East and North
The ranking differs from the per-order ranking — East leads on yearly totals while North leads on average order value — and the engine's table leaves the multi-year change column empty, consistent with only two calendar years of coverage. The commonest region value is South, at 25.7% of rows.
[CHART:4]
## Other findings: Units and revenue move together, almost mechanically
Across 300 rows, higher units goes with higher revenue, strongly: Spearman 0.976, 95% range 0.969 to 0.981. This is an association the engine will not call a cause, and the point is arithmetic as much as commercial — units top out at 40 and are integers, which the engine flags as possibly a capped or binned field rather than an exact item count.
[CHART:2]
[TABLE:2]
## Other findings: Units explains the revenue, region barely adds to it
A straight-line model of revenue from units and region, trained on earlier dates and scored on the 4 later blocks, predicts held-out orders with R squared 0.949 and a typical error of 91.1, against 475 for the mean of its training rows. Removing units drops R squared by 0.949; removing region drops it by 0.0139. The fitted effects are 44.7 per unit, and against the base region South −43.4, North 56.7, East 122, with 300 of 300 rows used and 240 scored. Because units and revenue rose together, the model is a strong description of one year's book and not evidence that region causes anything.
[TABLE:5]
## Other findings: Revenue is right-skewed, so a few orders move the averages
[CHART:3]
[TABLE:3]
## In the real world: outside demand was firm
US retail sales were up from the same period a year ago [S4], and the market outlook describes growth as tepid with sales resuming in late 2024 [S6] and a long-term projection of slow trend growth [S5]. Published eCommerce benchmarks put average order value by industry [S1] and globally [S2], with regional differences in shopping behaviour [S3] — but no currency is stated in the data, so the regional averages of 840 to 1,034 cannot be read against those benchmarks. The external trend is firm; the engine's intervals for this book of orders are too wide to confirm that 18.7% belongs to it.
## Risks and what the data cannot say
- The engine compares periods in observational data: a change it reports is an association with the period, not a finding about its cause.
- No forecast was made. The data cannot support a checkable forecast of monthly rows, monthly total revenue or monthly total units: there are 24 months of history and a checkable forecast needs at least 36 (12 to replay, the rest to learn from); about 12 more months would settle it.
- Not measured in this release: tipping points for the set-aside rows, which segments drive a change and reversals within them, and model-based probabilities; power is measured only at one size of true change (20%) in simulated conditions.
- My own: no currency is stated, product mix, customer type and discounting are absent, units top out at 40 as integers, and two calendar years cannot establish seasonality, multi-year extremes or a structural break.
## Scenarios
At the latest 12 months' level the run rate is 152,214 a year, or 12,684 in the average month, and each 1% of total revenue is worth 1,522 over a year; these carry the WATCH grade of the change they come from, so they describe the book, not a plan.
If West's units of the latest 12 months had sold at East's revenue per unit, the extra revenue would be +3,991: arithmetic, not a forecast.
## What to do
1. Treat +18.7% revenue and +1.6% units as watches, not planning inputs — the intervals run -32.1% to +86.2% and -51.6% to +65.2% — and extend the series by about 12 months to reach the 36 months a checkable monthly forecast needs.
2. Judge regions on medians alongside means, since the 90th percentile at 1,664 against a median of 926 means a few orders can produce the 194 North-West gap on their own.
3. Add product mix, customer type and discount fields before reporting the gap of 194 (95% range 17.3 to 387) as a regional difference, because the engine cannot separate a regional effect from what was sold.
4. Do not build regional targets on the fitted region effects (South −43.4; North 56.7; East 122) until they are tested against those controls — units alone accounts for R squared 0.949 of the fit and region only 0.0139.
